plain_english: If I wanted to break down this argument step by step with proof, I could show you many ways that busy people actually live the shortest lives of all. Fabianus wasn't one of those classroom philosophers — he was the real deal, old school. He used to say, "You have to attack your emotions head-on, not dance around them. Charge straight at them and break their lines. Don't just give them little scratches. I don't believe in playing word games with clever arguments. You have to crush these problems, not just poke at them." But if we want people to see their mistakes, we need to teach them, not just feel sorry for them.
original_excerpt: If I chose to divide this proposition into separate steps, supported by evidence, many things occur to me by which I could prove that the lives of busy men are the shortest of all. Fabianus, who was none of your lecture-room philosophers, but one of the true antique pattern, used to say, “We ought to fight against the passions by main force, not by skirmishing, and upset their line of battle by a home charge, not by inflicting trifling wounds: I do not approve of dallying with sophisms; they must be crushed, not merely scratched.” Yet, in order that sinners may be confronted with their errors, they must be taught, and not merely mourned for. Life is divided into three parts: that which has been, that which is, and that which is to come: of these three stages, that which we are passing through is brief, that which we are about to pass is uncertain, and that which we have passed is certain: this it is over which Fortune has lost her rights, and which can fall into no other man’s power: and this is what busy men lose: for they have no leisure to look back upon the past, and even if they had, they take no pleasure in remembering what they regret: they are, therefore, unwilling to turn their minds to the contemplation of ill-spent time, and they shrink from reviewing a course of action whose faults become glaringly apparent when handled a second time, although they were snatched at when we were under the spell of immediate gratification. No one, unless all his acts have been submitted to the infallible censorship of his own conscience, willingly turns his thoughts back upon the past.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 10

plain_english: Life has three parts: what's already happened, what's happening now, and what's yet to come. The present moment is brief. The future is uncertain. But the past is certain — it's the one thing Fortune can't touch, and no one else can control it. Yet this is exactly what busy people lose. They have no time to look back at their past. And even if they did have time, they wouldn't enjoy it. They'd just remember their regrets. So they refuse to think about the time they've wasted. They won't review their past actions because the mistakes become painfully obvious when you look back — even though those same actions seemed so appealing when they were caught up in the moment.
original_excerpt: He who has ambitiously desired, haughtily scorned, passionately vanquished, treacherously deceived, greedily snatched, or prodigally wasted much, must needs fear his own memory; yet this is a holy and consecrated part of our time, beyond the reach of all human accidents, removed from the dominion of Fortune, and which cannot be disquieted by want, fear, or attacks of sickness: this can neither be troubled nor taken away from one: we possess it for ever undisturbed. Our present consists only of single days, and those, too, taken one hour at a time: but all the days of past times appear before us when bidden, and allow themselves to be examined and lingered over, albeit busy men cannot find time for so doing. It is the privilege of a tranquil and peaceful mind to review all the parts of its life: but the minds of busy men are like animals under the yoke, and cannot bend aside or look back.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 10

plain_english: No one likes to look back at their past unless they can honestly say their conscience is clear. If you've been driven by ambition, looked down on others with pride, won through passion, deceived people, grabbed what you could, or wasted what you had — then of course you'll fear your own memories. But here's the thing: the past is actually sacred. It's the one part of our time that can't be touched by accidents, bad luck, poverty, fear, or illness. Nothing can disturb it or steal it from you. It's yours forever, completely safe.
original_excerpt: Consequently, their life passes away into vacancy, and as you do no good however much you may pour into a vessel which cannot keep or hold what you put there, so also it matters not how much time you give men if it can find no place to settle in, but leaks away through the chinks and holes of their minds. Present time is very short, so much so that to some it seems to be no time at all; for it is always in motion, and runs swiftly away: it ceases to exist before it comes, and can no more brook delay than can the universe or the host of heaven, whose unresting movement never lets them pause on their way. Busy men, therefore, possess present time, alone, that being so short that they cannot grasp it, and when they are occupied with many things they lose even this.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 10
